title: Google's Veo 2: Free Access to AI Video Generation
summary: Discover Google's Veo 2, a free AI tool for creating videos from text or images, revolutionizing content creation for all users.
body_text: Imagine a world where creating a video is as simple as typing a sentence or uploading an image. Thanks to Google's latest innovation, Veo 2, this is now a reality. Google has made the powerful AI video generation model, once exclusive to a paid partnership with Freepik, freely accessible to everyone through Google AI Studio. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Plivo (@go_plivo) Introducing Veo 2: A Leap in AI Video Generation Veo 2 represents a significant advancement in AI technology, offering users the ability to generate short, AI-driven videos using a simple text or image prompt. Google designed this model to democratize video creation, making it accessible to anyone with an internet connection. Previously, a paid integration with Freepik limited Veo 2's reach. Now, Google has opened the doors to creativity by making it freely available, allowing users to explore the potential of AI in video generation without the need for expensive tools or software. Veo 2 is here, first on Freepik worldwide Google partners with us to debut the most advanced AI video model. Unmatched realism, precision, and smooth animations. Run! The first 10K users will get 2 free generations. pic.twitter.com/9VaR4pOEQ3 — Freepik (@freepik) February 21, 2025 How Veo 2 Works The process is straightforward: users input a text or image prompt, and Veo 2 generates a video clip that lasts between 5 to 8 seconds. The model supports two aspect ratios, 16:9 for traditional widescreen and 9:16 for mobile-friendly vertical videos. While the resolution is capped below 1080p with a maximum frame rate of 24fps, the quality suffices for social media and quick content needs. "I'm late! I'm late! I'm late!" Veo 2 is the most amazing Gen AI piece of software I have ever seen. pic.twitter.com/dKR1V9FZ7j — Javi Lopez ⛩️ (@javilopen) January 12, 2025 Veo 2 allows users to generate up to two videos simultaneously, with a limit of nine generations every 24 hours. This setup ensures that while the service is free, it remains accessible and fair for all users. For those needing higher limits or commercial use, Veo 2 is available via the Vertex AI API at a cost of $0.50 per second, providing a scalable option for businesses and content creators. The Impact of Veo 2 on Content Creation With the advent of Veo 2, content creation is poised to undergo a transformation. The ability to quickly generate video content from simple prompts opens up new possibilities for marketers, educators, and storytellers. Imagine creating engaging video ads or educational snippets without the need for extensive video production skills. This democratization of video production particularly benefits small businesses and independent creators who can now compete on a more level playing field with larger organizations. The barrier to entry for high-quality video content significantly lowers, fostering innovation and creativity across various industries. Create mixed media style videos using GPT 4o and Veo 2, to animate a Vox style storytelling video tutorial and prompt for animation below 👇 pic.twitter.com/QaGvPYcTHN — Channel42 (@channel42_co) April 2, 2025 Conclusion Google's decision to make Veo 2 freely accessible marks a pivotal moment in the evolution of AI-driven content creation. By lowering the barriers to entry, Google empowers a new generation of creators to explore the potential of AI in video production. As we move forward, it's exciting to imagine how this technology will continue to shape the way we create and consume video content. What possibilities do you envision for the future of AI-driven video generation, and how might it transform the way we tell stories? ‍

title: Electrifying Logistics and Delivery Fleets
summary: Electrifying Logistics and Delivery Fleets
body_text: Now is an excellent time for commercial logistics and delivery fleets to transition to zero-emission electric vehicles (EVs) including vans, trucks and specialty vehicles instead of traditional gas or diesel-powered alternatives. Electric vehicles can significantly reduce operational costs, making them ideal for high-mileage commercial fleets like transport and delivery services. Fuel costs, a major expense in urban delivery routes characterized by frequent stop-and-go traffic, are considerably reduced with EVs. Additionally, EVs require minimal maintenance due to their simpler design with fewer moving parts and the absence of a combustion engine or oil. Another advantage is their ability to reduce noise pollution, making them an ideal choice for densely populated areas. Now substantial financial incentives, which offset a large portion of the initial purchase price of an EV, are playing a crucial role in accelerating the transition to electrification. The Transition to Electric Fleets Industry leaders in logistics and delivery are already making the move to electrification. For example, Amazon has been making significant strides in integrating electric vehicles into its delivery operations as part of its sustainability goals. The company has committed to deploying a large fleet of custom electric delivery vehicles, with thousands already in service. Amazon also recently made a major investment in electric heavy goods vehicles, adding a significant number of electric trucks to its fleet. Other logistics and delivery companies are adopting electric vehicles as part of their sustainability initiatives as well. For instance, some firms have incorporated EVs into their fleets and implemented solar-powered technologies to improve operational efficiency and reduce fuel consumption. These efforts represent a broader shift across the logistics industry toward environmentally friendly practices. There are numerous advantages to using EVs for commercial fleets. Logistics fleets can significantly cut fuel expenses while avoiding the unpredictability of fluctuating fuel prices. Electric vehicles (EVs) equipped with electric drivetrains require less maintenance and offer greater longevity compared to traditional combustion engine vehicles. EVs also operate with less noise and vibration, making them ideal for early-morning or late-night deliveries and improving comfort for drivers on long hauls. Features like regenerative braking help capture and reuse energy lost during braking, extending a vehicle’s range, particularly in stop-and-go traffic. Combined with improved battery technology, many commercial electric vehicles now offer up to 150 miles per charge, a distance far greater than the daily mileage driven by most delivery vehicles. Financial Incentives The financial rationale for electrifying commercial delivery fleets is also extremely compelling, with several states offering substantial financial rebates or tax credits that reduce upfront purchase costs. “Today, there is increasing demand across the United States to electrify delivery fleets, spurred by incentives at the state and federal level,” said Jason Maddox, President of Envirotech Vehicles . Envirotech is a provider of new zero-emission, purpose-built electric vehicles for commercial and last-mile delivery fleets, school districts, public and private transportation service companies, colleges and universities. Noteworthy programs include California’s Hybrid and Zero-Emission Truck and Bus Voucher Incentive Project (HVIP), which offers significant rebates on the base vehicle ranging from $20,000 to $240,000 depending on the type of vehicle purchased. The New Jersey Zero Emission Incentive Program (NJ ZIP) offers vouchers towards the purchase of new, zero emission vehicles ranging from $20,000 to $175,000, depending on the class of vehicle. NJ ZIP is a $90 million voucher pilot launched by the New Jersey Economic Development Authority (NJEDA) for medium and heavy duty zero-emission vehicles. The pilot is funded by the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative proceeds allocated to NJEDA for the purposes of reducing harmful emissions, particularly in communities disproportionately impacted by transportation emissions and creating economic opportunity within the state. “Thanks to California’s HVIP and New Jersey’s NJ ZIP incentives, small business owners in those states can significantly reduce the upfront costs to purchase electric vans and trucks,” said Maddox. Maddox adds that Texas, New York, Oregon, Washington and Colorado are among the states also offering rebates for commercial EVs. Additionally, countries like Canada provide a range of subsidies and incentives to support similar initiatives. The advantages of electrifying commercial fleets combined with these incentives are spurring early interest and orders. As an example, Osceola, Arkansas based Envirotech Vehicles announced in January 2025 that it has taken orders for vehicles for customers that have been awarded vouchers under the New Jersey Zero Emission Incentive Program. U.S. based manufacturers like Envirotech have moved beyond concepts and early prototypes to full production. Like the most popular consumer electric vehicles, Envirotech’s vehicles utilize a combination of aluminum for the body and high-strength steel in its construction. Aluminum reduces vehicle weight significantly, which means less energy is required to move the bus and increases vehicle range. A lighter vehicle also enhances acceleration, braking and handling. The aluminum body is 95% recyclable, much like a large soda can. To support these initiatives, Envirotech offers a variety of electric delivery vans and truck types that accommodate a range of delivery and logistics requirements and environments. Vans Various types of vans are available, including options for logistics, deliveries, passenger transportation and ADA-accessible vehicles. The compact size and maneuverability of logistics vans make them suitable for navigating narrow streets and congested urban areas. These vehicles are integral to supply chain operations, particularly for last-mile delivery, moving inventory between warehouses and serving retail and e-commerce operations. Cutaway vans typically feature a cab and chassis that can be modified into box trucks, shuttle buses, ambulances or other specialty vehicles. Their adaptability makes them popular in logistics, transportation and utility services. Urban trucks Urban trucks are medium-sized vehicles specifically built for city use, offering enough space for deliveries while being easy to drive through crowded streets. Their compact design and agility make them perfect for city centers with narrow roads and stop-and-go traffic. Urban trucks are highly suited for e-commerce and parcel services, efficiently handling large volumes of small package deliveries. They are also widely utilized for transporting goods to stores and customers within city areas. Additionally, compact vehicles designed for garbage and recycling collection cater specifically to urban environments. For construction purposes, these trucks are used to transport tools, materials and equipment to job sites located in cities. Right-hand drive vehicles are also available to facilitate a range of services such as delivering mail/packages on the curbside, garbage collection, street sweeping or for utility service operators who need better visibility or access to the curb. Specialty Vehicles A wide range of specialty vehicles are also available, including electric forklifts, sweepers and “Zipper” vehicles, a type of nimble vehicle used for efficient transport and management of goods within warehouses. Expanding Support and Infrastructure As the use of EVs expands across the US, the infrastructure needed to charge and support these vehicles is being installed across the country. In anticipation of the need, companies like Envirotech are helping to facilitate the rollout. As an example, in response to increased demand from NJ ZIP customers, the company has expanded the capability of its New Jersey service center in Manalapan, New Jersey by adding battery balancing and service equipment and capabilities. In addition, the service center features multi-point vehicle inspections and repairs, including tires and brakes. This will allow Envirotech customers to get vehicles repaired and back in service faster. “The transition to electric vehicles represents a pivotal opportunity for commercial logistics and delivery fleets,” said Maddox. “With substantial operational cost savings, reduced environmental impact and enhanced efficiency, EVs present a compelling case for businesses ready to innovate and align with modern sustainability goals.”

title: The Future of Lifted Trucks: Fox Factory Validates Hands-Free Driving
summary: Fox Factory makes hands-free driving possible on lifted trucks. Learn how F-150 and Silverado upfits retain full BlueCruise and Super Cruise compatibility.
body_text: It’s no secret that self-driving cars and Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) are already alive and well in the automotive market. Ford and Chevrolet have joined them with their release of the BlueCruise and Super Cruise technology for select vehicles. The manufacturers boast this technology reduces driver fatigue, making long road trips easier and more enjoyable. Fox Factory’s partnership with Ford and Chevrolet hasn’t been forgotten in this regard, with the lifted 2025 Ford F-150 and Chevrolet Silverado 1500 featuring BlueCruise/Super Cruise technology despite being modified. This makes Fox Factory Vehicles the first upfitter to validate hands-free compliance on lifted trucks! What does this mean for truck buyers? You no longer have to choose between performance upgrades and compatibility with cutting-edge, hands-free driving technology. (Image retrieved from media.ford.com ) What is Super Cruise or BlueCruise? So, how does all of this work? It may seem daunting to some to relinquish control over the steering wheel, but manufacturers have thought ahead! Thousands of miles of road are already mapped as Ford BlueCruise or GM Super Cruise compatible with a full network built for hands-free driving operation. For BlueCruise linked roads, Ford has a map tool to see if this technology has reached your area (check it out here!). However, that doesn’t mean you’re safe to take your eyes off the road just yet! Drivers will still have to facilitate lane changes by engaging the blinker or other indicators. Either way, this takes the standard cruise control up a notch by offering a hands-free and feet-off driving experience even for lifted trucks. Ford BlueCruise vs. GM Super Cruise Depending on whether you need BlueCruise to work when you’re towing, or want changing lanes to be autonomous, you may prefer one truck over the other. Let’s take a deeper dive and compare the two manufacturer technologies on the F150 and Silverado 1500: Feature Ford BlueCruise GM Super Cruise Mapped Road Coverage 130,000 miles (Hands-Free Blue Zones) 750,000 miles (Lidar-mapped highways) Lane Centering ✅ Keeps the truck centered ✅ More precise due to lidar mapping Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) ✅Maintains follow distance ✅ Maintains follow distance & executes lane changes Automatic Lane Changes ❌ Requires driver to use blinker ✅ Fully autonomous lane changes Works While Towing ❌ No ✅ Yes, but no autonomous lane changes while towing Sensor Tech Radar & cameras Lidar, HD GPS, cameras Driver Monitoring Cameras on steering column & dashboard Steering wheel light bar & driver-facing camera Reliability in Merging/Curves Still improving, can pinball between lanes More stable & confident lane control In 2024, Ford released a new version of its BlueCruise hands-free driving software, version 1.4, which allows for 2x - 5x the amount of time hands-free compared to version 1.2 and 1.3. The upgraded motion controller allows for better lane centering, as well as better handling in unfavorable conditions, tight curves, narrow lanes, and sun reflections. This version 1.4 technology will ship in the new 2025 Ford F-150 trucks, including the Fox Factory edition trucks in Black Widow or Rocky Ridge packages. (Image: Interior of Fox Factory Vehicles F150 during TRC testing) Hands-Free Driving on Lifted Trucks In general, the ADAS systems rely on calibrated sensors around the vehicle that may be disrupted with modifications such as a lift kit, bigger tires or suspension changes. However, Fox Factory Vehicles is the first to validate and retain compliance, ensuring the hands-free driving experience even with modifications. Fox Factory Vehicles partnered up with TRC Inc. to develop a customized, real-world testing program that specifically tested the ADAS functions in modified F-150 and Silverado trucks. The vehicles were measured in lane centering, Adaptive Cruise Control and Intelligent Speed Assist features. The results retained full functionality systems with the lift kits and other upfit modifications made to the trucks. (Image Above: Fox Factory Vehicles upfitted F150 during TRC testing) What This Means for You If having a “cool” looking truck matters to you but you’re also a tech geek that loves the idea of autonomous, hands-free driving, then Fox Factory Vehicles has your solution. You can have the lifted and modified truck of your dreams, while simultaneously being an active participant in the new frontier in driving tech. Here at Fox Factory Vehicles, we’re setting the standard along with our partners to shape the future of upfitted trucks. The Future of Upfitted Trucks is Hands-Free Fox Factory Vehicles is leading the way in making lifted trucks compatible with futuristic technologies such as BlueCruise and Super Cruise. Whether your dream truck is an F-150 or Silverado, you can experience high-end performance upgrades with cutting-edge technology. Don’t go anywhere though, Fox Factory Vehicles and our partners are just getting started. Ready to try out the BlueCruise or Super Cruise technology for yourself? Build your dream truck now or test drive at your local dealer Related Articles Fox Factory Vehicles: The Legacy Behind the Custom Truck Upfitter Why A Turnkey Custom Truck Is the Smarter Choice

title: Introducing BenchBB and the community paper of the Protein Design Competition
summary: We wrote a community paper about our Protein Design Competition, teaming up with your favourite protein designers from both rounds. We close the paper by creating BenchBB, the Bench-tested Binder Benc
body_text: Introducing BenchBB and the community paper of the Protein Design Competition We wrote a community paper about our Protein Design Competition, teaming up with your favourite protein designers from both rounds. We close the paper by creating BenchBB, the Bench-tested Binder Benc Adaptyv Bio Apr 26, 2025 TL;DR We wrote a community paper about our Protein Design Competition , teaming up with your favourite protein designers from both rounds. We aimed to explore the competition data in as many ways as we could, take stock of the state of the field, what SotAs have been established across the rounds, and which metric is most predictive of binding and expression. The one thing we kept meeting throughout: the lack of a standardized benchmark set for protein binder design , leading to difficult comparisons and a lack of consistent, high quality data. This is why we close the paper by creating BenchBB , the Bench -tested B inder B enchmark — a curated set of 7 protein targets designed to capture diverse binder design challenges by remaining accessible enough for wide scale lab validation. Want to read the community paper? Check it out on Biorxiv ! Want to test your protein-design model on BenchBB? Go to benchbb.bio and get started ! The community paper after the Protein Design Competition As you might remember, we hosted the Protein Design Competition . Briefly, we called for protein designers to create novel binders for EGFR and received over 1857 total submissions, 600 which we then experimentally tested in our lab, validating a total of 60 novel binders! For details you should check our previous blog posts . However, in these posts we could barely scratch the surface of possible data exploration. There was a strong demand to do more analyses and collect all the learnings , including those that our participants had already been doing throughout the rounds. The spirit of collaboration was strong throughout the competition so it did not seem fitting for us to act as the curators and gatekeepers for what would be included or said in such a writeup. Instead, we decided to form a consortium and launched an open call for collaboration . To our delight, several of the participants responded, and the excitement to contribute turned into a wide range of analyses, with people applying their expertise in different types of biomolecules (from antibodies to peptides), statistics, and general understanding of the current state of computational protein design, and vision for its future. The discussions in our Slack channel were some as delightful as they were interesting, and we finally distilled them into the preprint Crowdsourced Protein Design: Lessons From The Adaptyv EGFR Binder Competition . We will now summarize some of its key takeaways, but we strongly encourage you to read the full paper (honest clickbait: table 4 might surprise you!) In summary: More data = better metrics & models = better proteins We took another look at the data we had already analyzed in our blog posts , to see whether we can identify patterns and trends on the combined dataset of both rounds. While there was a sizeable increase in expression success and binder hit rate (see below), there remained many questions about when certain protein design approaches might be better than others and how to predict whether a protein makes a good binder from just the sequence alone. During the competition, we received many more protein designs than we could test in our lab during the timeframe of the contest. We thus had to select which designs to experimentally validate and which not. Our strategy was the following: We ranked designs by a set of computational metrics (ipAE, iPTM and ESM2 PLL) and chose the top 100 designs according to this ranking. We then additionally selected another 300 designs based on whether the protein designers had described a particularly interesting or novel design method. As we already suspected that the computational metrics might not correlate well with the binding affinity, this approach also rewarded protein designers for proposing new design methods that not just aimed at maximizing the computational score. In the paper, we run lots of statistical analyses to check the correlation of various surrogates (including iPTM, ipAE, and ESM 2/3/C) with binding strength and found that: at least on our dataset, ipAE, iPTM and ESM2 PLL (normalized or not) only correlate weakly with KD KD ​, despite some of them being part of the competition target metric. the good news, as Nikhil Haas (BioLM) had already noted , ESM3 and ESMC, when length normalized do correlate with KD KD ​, at least on our dataset. We don’t recommend you to rush towards blindly maximising this metric though, because as we show later in the paper, specific antibody domains might require different metrics to inform binder design — huge shoutout to Nikhil and the team at BioLM for donating both the data and their valuable time for making this analysis possible. Beyond this, there’s a lot more in the paper and the supplementary, e.g. a detailed study of the specific EGFR domains and their role in the successful binders, highlights of methods used throughout the competition (including Cradle’s winning entry , which they have been further evaluating and explaining in more detail in their own series of posts ) and more context on the competition and the community response . We thank all the authors for the time and resources they to get the paper done this way. However, the one thing that kept being said as we did all of these analyses and was confirmed with every insignificant p-value our analyses yielded is: we need more data. Thus, in the discussion we tried to acknowledge the great advances that became obvious as we looked back on the data, but also stress the limitations and challenges the field still faces: Computational metrics are getting better, but are not yet plug-and-play reliable , largely caused by the extremely non-standardized datasets they are derived from, often using different assays This lack of standardization extends as far as the definition of a binding hit , making it very difficult to compare results from one report to another Even if the assays and hit definitions were stable, everyone makes up their slightly tweaked sets of targets right now , with only a few if any targets being shared across studies. Of course, it is too easy to only complain about things, so we also suggest a first step in fixing this situation. Introducing BenchBB : the Bench-tested Binder Benchmark BenchBB is a curated set of 7 protein targets designed to provide a rigorous, consistent, and practical benchmark for computational binder design methods. While recent papers ( RFdiffusion , AlphaProteo , BindCraft ) have started to partially use a few common targets, the field lacks a standardized minimal set to objectively compare computational approaches. BenchBB directly addresses this gap. We selected targets by balancing multiple factors: Novel interfaces: the targets should not be heavily represented in standard ML training datasets. Challenging conformations: the targets have significant conformational changes and thus require varied binding mechanisms. Therapeutic relevance: target should have potential translational impact. Accessibility: ease of recombinant expression, primarily in E. coli , enabling broad lab validation. To ensure consistent, comparable evaluation across studies, we propose the following standardized assay approach for binding measurements: Use label-free sensing methods such as Bio-Layer Interferometry (BLI) or Surface Plasmon Resonance (SPR) to accurately measure kinetic parameters (kon, koff) and compute affinity constants (KD) from them. Whenever feasible, share assay parameters and conditions (e.g., sensor type, immobilization method, analyte concentration range, and fitting methods) as well as the raw kinetic data. Define a binder or “hit” as having a clearly measurable interaction signal with KD ≤ 10 µM. So let’s meet the 7 target proteins! This one needs no introduction - it was the catalyst that launched our entire competition . But, briefly, EGFR’s extracellular domain (~620 AA) binds EGF and TGF-α; it is frequently overexpressed or mutated in several cancers; and several therapeutic antibodies (e.g. Cetuximab) target it. PDB ID: 8HGO . We have accumulated a solid data set thanks to the participants in both competition rounds. Designers can further expand it or compare their tools or results to the data we have released - this is one of the main reasons to include EGFR. Cao et al. 2022 designed 50–65 aa miniproteins that bound EGFR’s Domain I and Domain III, successfully blocking EGF-induced signaling. They reported, however, an 0.01% hit-rate . We saw in the community paper how this was significantly improved upon: almost 3% in Round 1, then 13% in Round 2. And let’s not forget about the 8.2x binding affinity improvement over Cetuximab that Cradle achieved. IL7Ra is the alpha subunit of the IL-7 receptor (CD127), a 219 AA cytokine receptor critical for T-cell development . PDB ID: 3DI3 . Other than its therapeutic relevance (blocking IL-7/IL-7R interaction could modulate immune responses), we chose it because its “e ctodomain is easily produced in human cells and has been benchmarked in multiple prior studies” . RFdiffusion yielded multiple IL-7Rα binders where earlier Rosetta designs yielded almost none (original ~2.2% with AlphaFold selection to a reported ~34% for RFdiffusion). One designed binder showed nanomolar binding and inhibited IL-7 signaling in vitro . Cao et al. 2022 reported an 0.05% pre-AlphaFold hit-rate for de novo binders. AlphaProteo also generated strong IL-7Rα binders in one round. All these were de novo mini-proteins (~50–60 AA) that expressed well in E. coli and bound IL-7Rα with high affinity (comparable to or better than a natural IL-7:IL-7R interaction). They report a 24.5% success rate, greater than the remeasured RFdiffusion one (16.8% versus the original 34% published). PL-L1 is an immune checkpoint ligand (~290 AA) expressed on cancer cells and APCs. PD-L1 binds PD-1 on T cells, suppressing immune responses. PDB ID: 4Z18 . Gainza et al. 2023 noted PD-L1’s surface “displays a flat interface considered to be ‘hard to drug’ by small molecules”, thus making it ideal for testing advanced design methods. We consider it a “ de facto binder design benchmark target” RFdiffusion reported a 12.6% hit-rate. It was additionally benchmarked by AlphaProteo , MaSIF , BindCraft , and Yang et al., 2025 . BBF-14 is a de novo designed 112-residue β-barrel protein (13.8 kDa) with an internal hydrophobic pore. PDB ID: 9HAG . Serves as a stress-test for binder design on a novel, non-natural target. With BBF-14, there are no evolved binders or known epitopes – designers must rely solely on the computed structure. Thus, it “ can assess generalization beyond natural interfaces”. It was previously used as a target in the BindCraft paper , where one design (“binder4”) bound BBF-14 with KD KD ​ of 20.9 nM (SPR). BindCraft achieved a 55% hit-rate (6/11) on BBF-14. BHRF1 is a viral anti-apoptotic protein from Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) that mimics Bcl-2, allowing infected cells to evade apoptosis. It is associated with EBV-linked cancers . PDB ID: 2WH6 . Our main reasons for choosing were that it is “ easily expressed in E. coli and commercially available with many antibody controls”. Additionally, it has a known hydrophobic hotspot - the BH3-binding cleft , which restricts the search space. Targeted initially by Procko et al. 2014 - their de novo 86 AA minibinder (“BINDI”) could bind BHRF1 with 220 pM affinity (PDB ID: 4OYD ). More recently, AlphaProteo reported an 88% experimental hit-rate, far above prior methods, yielding multiple nanomolar binders without any optimization. MBP is a 42-kDa periplasmic binding protein in E. coli that binds maltose/maltodextrins as part of a sugar transport system. It is very stable and well-expressed; commonly used as an N-terminal fusion solubility tag to aid recombinant protein expression . PDB ID: 1PEB . MBP’s abundance and stability make it easy to produce and assay, thus it can be tested in any lab. Another reasons for choosing it is that it f eatures “a well-characterized active site allowing straightforward binder screening via elution from amylose resin”. Zhou et al. 2025 employed de novo design and computational screening to create MBP binders: “6 candidate binders targeting MBP” were identified without any directed evolution. These hits were small folded proteins (≈80–100 aa) that bound MBP with low micromolar to nanomolar affinity. This RNA-guided DNA endonuclease needs to further introduction - it the key in CRISPR gene editing, widely used in gene editing and any genomic biotechnology application. PDB ID: 4OO8 . We chose it for its “ easy structural characterization via cryoEM; stable, easily expressed in E. coli, and with multiple known binding sites and conformations”. Cas9’s size and moving parts make binder design difficult, but a successful binder can act as an “off-switch” for genome editing ( de novo binders regulating the enzyme function). The BindCraft authors note including “multi-domain nucleases, such as CRISPR-Cas9” as challenging targets. Used as a target for BindCraft - where a small designed protein binder (~100 AA) bound Cas9 and inhibited its genome editing activity. Surprisingly, it also yielded a 100% hit-rate, with the best binder measuring a KD KD ​ of 267 nM (SPR). Next steps Want to read the full paper? Check it out on Biorxiv ! Want to test your protein-design model on BenchBB? Go to benchbb.bio and get started ! Got questions about the paper or BenchBB? Just email us at benchbb@adaptyvbio.com Acknowledgements Thanks to all the consortium authors for joining us throughout this journey, their contribution to the paper and in-depth discussions over the benchmark targets! title: Learning management systems (LMS): 6 key features and top use cases
summary: An LMS is software used to deliver, track, report, and manage educational courses, training, or learning and development programs.
body_text: Learning management systems are a foundation of learning programs at educational institutions, corporations, and nonprofits. Learn about the key capabilities of LMS platforms and how advanced features like interactive learning, video, and AI improve engagement and learning outcomes. What is a learning management system (LMS)? A learning management system (LMS) is a software application that delivers, tracks, reports, and manages educational courses, training programs, or learning and development programs. It provides a centralized platform for all learning activities, allowing users to access courses and educational materials, complete assessments, and track progress over time. LMSs are used in various sectors, including educational institutions, corporate environments, government organizations, and nonprofits, to enable training, personal, and professional development. LMSs offer functionalities such as delivering learning content, assessing students or trainees, tracking progress, and generating detailed reports. Systems also provide features like personalized learning paths, interactive learning and multimedia content, integration with other enterprise systems, and multi-device support. LMSs are a driving force behind the evolution of digital learning and have become a crucial infrastructure for remote education and training, powering millions of learning experiences worldwide. This is part of an extensive series of guides about IaaS . Key features of modern LMS platforms Let’s review the capabilities typically provided by a full-featured LMS platform. 1. eLearning assessment tools Assessments are a crucial component of any learning program, allowing organizations to measure learner comprehension and knowledge retention. An LMS should offer a variety of assessment tools, including: Interactive assessments like quizzes, multiple-choice tests, and interactive case studies. Automated grading features can save instructors time while providing immediate feedback to learners. Adaptive assessments , which adjust difficulty levels based on user performance, ensure a personalized evaluation process. Gamification elements such as timed challenges, leaderboards, and scenario-based simulations make evaluations more engaging. Peer assessments and instructor feedback mechanisms to enable collaborative learning and continuous improvement. A comprehensive assessment system ensures that learners complete their courses and gain meaningful knowledge that translates into real-world skills. 2. Interactive learning tools Interactive learning elements keep learners engaged and enhance knowledge retention. An LMS should include: Online communication tools like discussion forums, live chat, and social learning features. These tools encourage collaboration among peers, allowing users to share insights, ask questions, and participate in group discussions. Multimedia-based content , including videos, simulations, and virtual reality (VR) training modules. Interactive content keeps learners actively engaged, making complex concepts easier to understand. Interactive learning features such as branching scenarios and role-playing exercises further enhance the learning experience by providing hands-on practice. By incorporating interactive tools, organizations can create an engaging and immersive learning environment that maximizes learner participation. 3. AI and automation tools Artificial intelligence (AI) and automation enhance LMS functionality by personalizing learning experiences and streamlining administrative tasks. AI-driven recommendation engines analyze learner behavior to suggest relevant courses, ensuring users receive tailored training based on their interests and career goals. Additionally, AI-powered chatbots provide instant support, answering common queries and guiding users through the platform. Automation features reduce the administrative burden by handling repetitive tasks such as course enrollments, reminders, and progress tracking. For example, an LMS can automatically assign training modules based on job roles, send completion reminders, and generate performance reports. AI-driven analytics also help identify trends and learning patterns, enabling organizations to optimize their training strategies. By leveraging AI and automation, businesses can improve efficiency while delivering a more personalized and effective learning experience. 4. Reports and analytics An LMS should provide detailed reports and analytics to help administrators track learner progress, course completion rates, assessment scores, and overall engagement. These insights allow organizations to evaluate the effectiveness of their training programs and make data-driven improvements. Real-time dashboards offer a visual representation of key metrics, making it easy to identify trends and areas where learners may be struggling. Customizable reporting features allow administrators to generate tailored reports that meet specific compliance or performance tracking needs. 5. Content management and organization A robust LMS offers efficient tools to manage and organize learning content. This includes capabilities to create, store, categorize, and update digital course materials in various formats such as text, video, PDFs, and SCORM-compliant packages. Key features include: Course structuring tools that allow administrators to break content into modules, lessons, or topics for better organization and learner navigation. Content versioning and update management to ensure learners always access the most current materials. Tagging and categorization to support easy search, discovery, and reuse of learning assets. Access control to manage who can view, edit, or publish content, ensuring security and role-based customization. Efficient content organization not only improves the learner experience but also helps maintain consistency and quality across training programs. 6. Virtual classrooms and video conferencing Virtual classrooms are essential for real-time, instructor-led training in an LMS. Integrated video conferencing tools enable live sessions, webinars, and collaborative discussions, replicating a classroom experience in an online environment. Important capabilities include: Real-time video and audio communication with support for screen sharing, breakout rooms, and interactive whiteboards. Scheduling and calendar integration to manage live sessions and send reminders to participants. Session recording and playback for learners to review content on demand. Attendance tracking and participation analytics to monitor learner engagement. These tools support synchronous learning, facilitate direct interaction between instructors and learners, and enhance engagement in remote or hybrid training setups. Types of learning management systems Let’s review four types of learning management systems, to understand which type of LMS is best suited for your organization. 1. Cloud-based (SaaS) LMS Cloud-based LMSs, typically offered as software-as-a-service (SaaS), host the LMS externally and provide access via the internet. This model offers advantages such as scalability, ease of access, and reduced internal IT costs. Users can access the LMS from anywhere with an internet connection. Security and updates are typically handled by the service provider, ensuring that the system is always up-to-date. Setup and deployment are generally quick and straightforward since the infrastructure needs minimal onsite management. This type of LMS can be particularly beneficial for organizations looking to quickly implement and manage online learning without heavy IT resources. 2. Self-hosted LMS Self-hosted LMSs involve the software being hosted on an organization’s own servers, offering greater control over data and customization. Organizations can modify the system according to their specific requirements, allowing for a tailored learning environment. This option can be more cost-effective in the long term but requires a dedicated IT team for maintenance and support. Deployment of a self-hosted LMS might involve a longer timeframe and upfront cost, as it requires purchasing hardware and creating infrastructure. Organizations choose this model when data security is a priority and when they want to integrate the LMS with other internal systems. Despite these challenges, the ability to customize the LMS and have direct control over learning resources and data makes it a preferred choice for larger enterprises or educational institutions. 3. Open-source LMS Open-source LMSs offer organizations the ability to download, modify, and distribute the platform freely, with the primary advantage being cost-effectiveness. These systems provide significant flexibility for customization, enabling institutions to adapt the software to meet specific needs and integrate new functionalities as required. However, leveraging open-source LMSs involves some challenges. Organizations must have the technical capability to install and maintain the system, which could be resource-intensive. With no direct vendor support, handling system updates and security patches may require considerable IT expertise. Despite these challenges, open-source LMSs are favored by organizations prioritizing control over their learning environments while minimizing software costs. 4. Enterprise LMS Enterprise LMSs are for large-scale organizations seeking training solutions that integrate with other business applications. These systems are built to handle large user bases, complex organizational hierarchies, and diverse learning needs. They often feature advanced analytics, sophisticated reporting tools, and capabilities for compliance management, making them especially suitable for regulated sectors like healthcare and finance. Due to their extensive functionality, enterprise LMSs require considerable investment regarding setup and ongoing management. However, they can streamline the training process and enable continuous learning across large corporations. These systems enable organizations to efficiently administer training programs and monitor progress, crucial for maintaining a skilled and up-to-date workforce. LMS usability and accessibility In order to be effective, an LMS must be easy to use, available to its audience via the devices they use, accessible to learners with physical disabilities, and able to integrate with existing systems in the organization. Intuitive user interface An intuitive user interface (UI) is critical for ensuring smooth navigation and usability within an LMS. A well-structured layout with clear menus, course categorization, and logical workflows reduces the learning curve for both learners and administrators. When users can easily locate their courses, track progress, and access support resources, they are more likely to stay engaged and complete their training. For administrators, an intuitive UI streamlines course creation, enrollment management, and reporting tasks. Features such as drag-and-drop course builders, automated notifications, and search-friendly content libraries improve efficiency and reduce the time spent on administrative work. A good LMS should also support branding customization, allowing organizations to incorporate logos, color schemes, and company themes for a cohesive learning experience. Responsive design and mobile compatibility A responsive LMS is essential for modern learning environments, as users increasingly access courses on different devices, including desktops, tablets, and smartphones. A well-designed LMS should automatically adjust its layout and features to fit various screen sizes, ensuring a seamless experience regardless of the device being used. This flexibility is particularly beneficial for remote employees, field workers, and students who may need to complete coursework on the go. Mobile-friendly LMSs often include downloadable content and offline access capabilities, allowing learners to continue training even without an internet connection. Mobile compatibility also enhances learner engagement by enabling microlearning—short, easily digestible training sessions that fit into busy schedules. Push notifications, mobile quizzes, and bite-sized video lessons make learning more accessible and interactive. Accessibility features An LMS should adhere to accessibility standards such as the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) to ensure that learning materials are accessible to all users, including those with disabilities. Key accessibility features include: Screen reader compatibility Keyboard navigation Adjustable text sizes Closed captions for videos Transcripts for audio content Alternative text for images These measures ensure that visually and hearing-impaired learners can fully engage with training material. Beyond technical features, an LMS should allow administrators to create content that accommodates diverse learning needs. For example, customizable pacing options let learners adjust the speed of video content, while alternative content formats (such as text, audio, and interactive elements) cater to different learning styles. Integration capabilities A well-integrated LMS should seamlessly connect with other enterprise systems such as HR software, customer relationship management (CRM) platforms, video conferencing tools, and content management systems (CMS). Integration with HR systems enables automatic enrollment of new employees into relevant training programs, ensuring a smooth onboarding experience. Additionally, linking the LMS with a CRM allows organizations to provide sales and customer support teams with relevant training based on client interactions. API support and single sign-on (SSO) capabilities further enhance the LMS experience by streamlining authentication and data exchange across platforms. Integrations with third-party content providers such as LinkedIn Learning or Coursera expand course offerings without requiring additional content development. Learning management system vs. learning experience platform: what is the difference? While a Learning Management System (LMS) like Moodle or Blackboard focuses on managing and delivering structured learning programs, a Learning Experience Platform (LXP) like Adobe Learning Manager or 360Learning provides a more personalized and engaging learning experience. The key differences between an LMS and an LXP include: Content structure: An LMS follows a top-down approach where administrators control content distribution, while an LXP enables learners to explore and curate content based on their interests and learning needs. User experience: LMSs prioritize compliance, assessments, and tracking, whereas LXPs emphasize engagement, social learning, and content discovery. AI and personalization: LXPs leverage artificial intelligence (AI) to recommend content tailored to individual learners, while LMSs focus on delivering standardized training programs. Integration: LMSs are often integrated with enterprise systems for HR and compliance training, while LXPs integrate with various content sources such as blogs, videos, and third-party learning platforms. Ultimately, an LMS is best suited for organizations that need structured training and compliance management, whereas an LXP is ideal for companies that want to foster a continuous learning culture with user-driven content discovery. Benefits of using a learning management system Implementing a Learning Management System (LMS) provides the following advantages for organizations and educational institutions: Centralized learning platform – An LMS consolidates all learning materials, courses, and training resources in one place, making it easier to manage and access educational content. Improved accessibility – Learners can access courses anytime and from anywhere, facilitating remote learning and enabling flexible learning schedules. Efficient tracking and reporting – Administrators and instructors can monitor learner progress, generate reports, and analyze performance data to optimize training programs. Automated training processes – LMSs automate tasks such as course enrollments, assessments, certifications, and notifications, reducing administrative workload. Scalability – Organizations can easily expand their training programs by adding new courses, increasing users, or integrating with other systems without significant infrastructure changes. Cost-effectiveness – Reduces the costs associated with traditional in-person training, such as travel, printed materials, and instructor fees. Engagement and collaboration features – Discussion forums, gamification, and interactive content foster a more engaging learning experience, encouraging collaboration among learners. Use cases and examples for learning management systems Here are some of the common industry use cases for LMS platforms. 1. Education In education, LMSs are widely adopted as part of the eLearning infrastructure in schools and higher education institutions. They enable the delivery of online and blended courses, expanding access to education beyond the confines of a traditional classroom. Features such as interactive forums, multimedia lessons, and virtual classrooms enrich the learning experience, fostering engagement among students. Educators benefit from the ability to distribute assignments, assess student performance, and provide feedback through the LMS, reducing administrative burdens. Furthermore, LMSs support diverse learning styles by offering varied content formats, helping to cater to each student’s unique needs and preferences. The use of analytics within educational LMSs also allows institutions to refine curriculums based on data-driven insights, enhancing educational outcomes overall. 2. Corporate training In the corporate sphere, LMSs are crucial for managing employee training and development programs. Organizations employ them to onboard new employees, teach new skills, and ensure compliance with mandatory regulatory standards. By using LMSs, companies can uniformly distribute training materials, standardizing training outcomes across diverse geographical locations. Furthermore, corporate LMSs support upskilling initiatives by offering continuous learning opportunities, thereby enhancing employee engagement and retention. The customization capabilities of these systems allow organizations to tailor learning paths to align with career progression. As a result, businesses can maintain a competitive edge by keeping their workforce well-equipped and knowledgeable. Learn more in our detailed guide to corporate learning management system (coming soon) 3. Government and nonprofits Government bodies and nonprofits utilize LMSs to provide training that aligns with compliance, efficiency, and capacity-building needs. An LMS allows these entities to train staff uniformly, ensuring consistency in knowledge and compliance with regulations. For nonprofits, LMSs offer a cost-effective solution for disseminating educational resources across their network of volunteers and stakeholders. The ability to customize and integrate specific training modules enables these organizations to address the unique challenges they face while improving the quality of service delivery. Additionally, LMSs support multilingual capabilities and inclusivity, ensuring that training is accessible to diverse populations, and meeting the operational needs of both government and nonprofit organizations. 4. Healthcare LMS platforms play a critical role in the healthcare sector by facilitating continuous education, compliance training, and professional development for medical professionals. Healthcare organizations use LMSs to ensure staff members remain up-to-date with the latest medical practices, regulatory requirements, and patient care protocols. With features like certification tracking, automated course assignments, and interactive learning modules, LMSs help medical staff efficiently complete required training and maintain licensure. Additionally, LMSs support scenario-based learning and virtual simulations, allowing healthcare professionals to practice clinical procedures and improve decision-making skills in a risk-free environment. Beyond training healthcare workers, LMSs are also utilized for patient education. Hospitals and clinics provide online learning materials through an LMS to help patients understand medical conditions, treatment plans, and post-operative care procedures. This educational approach improves patient engagement, encourages adherence to prescribed treatments, and improves overall health outcomes. Learn more in our detailed guide to learning management system healthcare (coming soon) Best practices for successfully implementing an LMS Here are a few tips that can help your organization successfully adopt and implement an LMS system. 1. Define clear learning objectives Before implementing an LMS, organizations should establish clear learning objectives that align with business goals or educational outcomes. These objectives should define what learners are expected to achieve and how training success will be measured. Without a well-defined purpose, an LMS implementation can become disorganized, leading to low engagement and ineffective training programs. To set clear objectives, organizations should assess learner needs, identify skill gaps, and determine the type of content required. Whether the goal is employee onboarding, compliance training, or professional development, objectives should be specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound (SMART). 2. Ensure user training and support A successful LMS implementation requires that both learners and administrators are properly trained on how to use the system. Without adequate support, users may struggle with navigation, leading to frustration and low adoption rates. Providing onboarding sessions, user guides, and interactive tutorials can help users become comfortable with the platform. In addition to initial training, organizations should offer ongoing support through a help desk, chatbots, or a dedicated support team. A knowledge base with FAQs and video tutorials can also empower users to troubleshoot common issues independently. Ensuring that users have access to the necessary resources will boost engagement, improve learning outcomes, and ultimately, improve the return on investment (ROI) of the LMS. 3. Plan for content development and migration Content is at the core of any LMS, so organizations should have a clear strategy for developing and migrating learning materials. If transitioning from a previous system, it’s essential to evaluate existing content for relevance, update outdated materials, and ensure compatibility with the new LMS. Poorly planned content migration can lead to data loss, broken links, and inconsistent training experiences. For new content development, organizations should consider a mix of multimedia formats such as videos, quizzes, interactive modules, and gamification elements to enhance engagement. Leveraging SCORM or xAPI-compliant content ensures compatibility across different LMS platforms. A well-structured content strategy will help organizations deliver high-quality, effective training that meets the needs of diverse learners. 4. Focus on user experience and accessibility A user-friendly and accessible LMS is crucial for ensuring high engagement and inclusivity. The platform should have an intuitive interface that makes it easy for learners to navigate courses, track progress, and access resources without confusion. When customizing an LMS, teams should be careful to avoid creating complex or cluttered user experiences. Additionally, accessibility should be a priority to accommodate learners with disabilities. Features such as screen reader compatibility, keyboard navigation, closed captions for videos, and adjustable font sizes ensure compliance with Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG). By prioritizing user experience and accessibility, organizations create an inclusive learning environment that benefits all users. 5. Monitor and analyze learning analytics Implementing an LMS is not just about delivering content—it’s also about tracking learner progress and optimizing training effectiveness. Organizations should regularly monitor key metrics such as course completion rates, engagement levels, and assessment scores to identify areas for improvement. Advanced LMS platforms offer real-time dashboards and predictive analytics to help administrators make data-driven decisions. By analyzing learning data, organizations can refine training programs, personalize learning paths, and address learner challenges proactively. Regular feedback from users should also be incorporated to enable continuous improvement of training programs. How Kaltura enhances LMS engagement with interactive learning and video content Traditional learning management systems (LMS) often struggle with engagement, interactivity, and seamless content integration. Kaltura transforms LMS platforms into all-in-one scalable, dynamic, and measurable learning environments by leveraging video-based learning, interactive content, and AI-driven insights. Kaltura empowers educators and trainers to deliver live, on-demand, and interactive video-based learning experiences that fully integrate into their existing LMS and workflows. With features like VOD libraries, certification, media editing and repurposing, AI personalized learning paths, and a fully equipped engagement suite, learners stay engaged while instructors gain actionable insights into performance and participation. This ensures that learning is not just passive consumption but an interactive and immersive experience. Whether through AI-powered captioning, or advanced analytics, Kaltura ensures that training is accessible, engaging, and personalized. By embedding these features directly into your LMS, Kaltura helps organizations drive better learning outcomes and improve retention rates. Learn more about Kaltura’s LMS video platform integrations

title: Kenvue new infant skin care research focuses on sensitive skin at the 15th World Congress of Pediatric Dermatology
body_text: Pediatricians and pediatric dermatologists from around the world are gathering in Buenos Aires, Argentina, April 8-11 for the 15th World Congress of Pediatric Dermatology (WCPD 2025). What better place to talk about the science behind the Kenvue platform of iconic pediatric skincare brands and their evolving science for every stage of childhood? The Company will share brand new findings on baby skin conditions ranging from sensitive skin to eczema, and how to best care for these skin types. “We never stop advancing the science of skincare for the tiniest patients. That’s why we’re showcasing findings from our latest studies, including ways to improve infants’ fragile skin barrier and diminish the physical and emotional impacts of eczema,” said Karina Ribeiro, Global Head of R&D, Essential Health at Kenvue. “Kenvue will also host a panel of globally renowned experts to discuss infant skin care and bathing, with best practices from around the world. It’s part of our commitment to helping pediatricians determine the right skin care for their patients during those key stages of development.” The symposium, “Dear Doctor: Advice on Skin Care and Bathing Essentials from Birth” will be held on Tuesday, April 8 from 12:30 – 2:00 p.m. in Room F of the Centro de Convenciones Buenos Aires. A panel of experts including Lawrence Eichenfield, MD, Chief of Pediatric and Adolescent Dermatology at Rady Children’s Hospital, Arun Inamadar, MD, Professor at Shri B. M. Patil Medical College Hospital and Research Centre, Ana Mósca, MD, Associate Clinical Professor of Pediatric Dermatology at Hospital Municipal Jesus, and Mauricio Torres-Pradilla, MD, Professor at Foundation University of Health Sciences, will discuss the latest research and best practices for bathing, moisturizing, and managing sensitive skin in babies. Spanish translation will be provided. In three brand-new scientific studies authored by Gabrielle Kosmoski, Kenvue R&D Baby Claims & Clinical Manager, the company focuses on essential skincare for infants, including sensitive skin: Baby Gentle Wash & Moisturizing Lotion Newborn Routine: Improves Skin Condition and Positively Impacts Skin Barrier, Microbiome, & Bonding, poster #732 — Newborns’ skin barrier is vulnerable to dryness and irritation. Over the course of 4 weeks, a gentle wash and lotion routine improved irritation, dryness, overall skin appearance, and skin pH. Baby Eczema Regimen Provides Clinical Eczema Improvement and Skin Benefits in subjects with Mild to Moderate Eczema, poster #728 — For babies, eczema’s effects are both physical and emotional. Products with colloidal oat helped improve the skin condition of babies of all skin tones/types with mild to moderate eczema. Eczema severity, eczema lesions, skin hydration, and skin barrier function were improved, as were babies’ overall comfort and mood. Clinical Improvement in Moisturization and Skin Moisture Barrier of an Emollient-Rich Balm Compared to a Lotion and Cream, poster #723 — Early emollient use is critical for baby’s skin development. A thick, emollient-rich balm with oat improved moisturization and barrier function better than a lotion and cream, while acting as a protective layer reducing trans-epidermal water loss and fortifying the skin barrier. To learn more about the research or schedule interviews, please contact Kenvue R&D media relations. title: TAL Education Group Announces Unaudited Financial Results for the Fourth Fiscal Quarter and the Fiscal Year 2025
summary: /PRNewswire/ -- TAL Education Group (NYSE: TAL) ("TAL" or the "Company"), a smart learning solutions provider in China, today announced its unaudited financial...
body_text: BEIJING , April 24, 2025 /PRNewswire/ -- TAL Education Group (NYSE: TAL ) ("TAL" or the "Company"), a smart learning solutions provider in China , today announced its unaudited financial results for the fourth quarter and the fiscal year ended February 28, 2025 . Highlights for the Fourth Quarter of Fiscal Year 2025 Net revenues were US$610.2 million , compared to net revenues of US$429.6 million in the same period of the prior year. Loss from operations was US$16.0 million , compared to loss from operations of US$11.1 million in the same period of the prior year. Non-GAAP loss from operations, which excluded share-based compensation expenses, was US$1.7 million , compared to non-GAAP income from operations of US$9.4 million in the same period of the prior year. Net loss attributable to TAL was US$7.3 million , compared to net income attributable to TAL of US$27.5 million in the same period of the prior year. Non-GAAP net income attributable to TAL, which excluded share-based compensation expenses, was US$7.0 million , compared to non-GAAP net income attributable to TAL of US$48.0 million in the same period of the prior year. Basic and diluted net loss per American Depositary Share ("ADS") were both US$0.01 . Non-GAAP basic and diluted net income per ADS, which excluded share-based compensation expenses, were both US$0.01 . Three ADSs represent one Class A common share. Cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments totaled US$3,618.4 million as of February 28, 2025 , compared to US$3,303.3 million as of February 29, 2024 . Highlights for the Fiscal Year Ended February 28, 2025 Net revenues were US$2,250.2 million , compared to net revenues of US$1,490.4 million in the prior year. Loss from operations was US$3.2 million , compared to loss from operations of US$69.2 million in the prior year. Non-GAAP income from operations, which excluded share-based compensation expenses, was US$61.8 million , compared to non-GAAP income from operations of US$19.7 million in the prior year. Net income attributable to TAL was US$84.6 million , compared to net loss attributable to TAL of US$3.6 million in the prior year. Non-GAAP net income attributable to TAL, which excluded share-based compensation expenses, was US$149.5 million , compared to non-GAAP net income attributable to TAL of US$85.3 million in the prior year. Basic and diluted net income per ADS were both US$0.14 . Non-GAAP basic and diluted net income per ADS, which excluded share-based compensation expenses, were US$0.25 and US$0.24 , respectively. Extension of Share Repurchase Program by the Company The Company's board of directors (the "Board") has authorized to extend the Company's share repurchase program (the "Share Repurchase Program") initially launched in April 2021 by another 12 months. The Company has repurchased its ADSs, every three representing one Class A common share, at an aggregate consideration of approximately US$13.1 million under the Share Repurchase Program between April 1, 2024 and April 24, 2025 . Pursuant to the extended Share Repurchase Program, the Company may repurchase up to approximately US$490.7 million of its common shares through April 30, 2026 . The share repurchases may be effected from time to time on the open market at prevailing market prices, in privately negotiated transactions, in block trades and/or through other legally permissible means, depending on market conditions and will be implemented in accordance with applicable rules and regulations. The Company expects to fund the repurchases out of its existing cash balance. Board Member Changes The Board has appointed Mr. Yi Wang as an independent director, effective April 22, 2025 . Mr. Wang will also serve as Chair of the Compensation Committee and as a member of both the Audit Committee and the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. Dr. Weiru Chen has resigned from the Board and all Board committees for personal reasons. Dr. Chen will continue to support the Company in an advisory capacity. "We are pleased to welcome Mr. Wang to the Board of TAL. Mr. Wang brings extensive experience across both the business and education sectors, and we are confident that his insights will further strengthen TAL's strategic direction, governance, and operational excellence," said Mr. Bangxin Zhang, Founder, Chairman of the Board, and Chief Executive Officer of TAL, "We also want to express our deep appreciation to Dr. Weiru Chen for his outstanding service and invaluable contributions over the past decade. We look forward to continuing our collaboration with Dr. Chen in his new advisory role." Since 2014, Mr. Wang has served as the Executive Director of the Harvard Center Shanghai, where he oversees Harvard University's initiatives and programs in China . Prior to his role at Harvard , Mr. Wang held significant positions in the corporate sector, including Managing Director at Goldman Sachs and Partner at McKinsey & Company. He also served the financial industry as an independent director of Citibank ( China ) from 2017 to 2023. In addition to his professional endeavors, Mr. Wang is deeply committed to education-related charitable work. He is the co-founder and Vice Chair of the Board of UWC Changshu China and a founding board member of Tsinglan School in Dongguan, China . title: Learning to learn: How I transitioned from engineering PhD to Chief Product Officer
summary: Beacons is a free, all-in-one platform with the best link in bio, media kit builder, online store and email marketing tool for creators on Instagram + Tiktok
body_text: Neal, our CEO, led product during the earliest stages of our company. Before a company finds any semblance of traction, figuring out the product is the core problem to be solved. David, our CTO, was focused on implementing the product vision at a lower level of the technical stack. At various points of Beacons' life, I've worked as an engineer, a data scientist, a designer, a user researcher, a growth lead, a social media manager, and a customer success specialist. I sat in the middle layer between Neal and David. Over time, this middle layer became product, which I took on as Chief Product Officer. Today, I'm leveraging all the skills and context I've acquired to determine what we should build and why. Although I haven't had any professional experience working in a product role prior to Beacons, I was able to grow quickly by allocating 80% of my time to executing and 20% of my time to learning. I was privileged to have access to some incredible resources: My team: Neal and David were in tandem consuming content about building good product. They pushed me to create frameworks and mental models for prioritizing and visualizing different parts of the product roadmap. Reading: In addition to staying generally knowledgeable about the creator space through creator newsletters, Twitter, and users interviews, I subscribed to product newsletters like Lenny's Newsletter and Bring the Donuts. Users: I spent lots of time doing user interviews to develop more authentic user empathy. Friends: I reached out to friends who were product managers and employees at big tech companies and growing startups. I learned from them that product is all about people: aligning stakeholders, communicating the strategy, and making sure everyone feels heard and taken care of. Reflection: I carved out regular time to reflect on what worked and what didn't work. Building Beacons has been the most challenging and rewarding experience of my life. Here are a few key takeaways from this crazy journey: Prioritize personal growth and wellbeing . Throughout my life but especially since starting Beacons, I've loved building personal processes through journaling making sure I do something positive for my physical and mental health daily reflecting on a set of questions each week to ensure, at a macro level, I'm moving in the direction I want in life The best thing you can do for the people in your life is make sure you're healthy and present for them. Maintaining these habits even through the busiest times at Beacons is crucial for making me better at work. Consistency and discipline are the foundation of everything . When building startups, you go through phases where nothing seems to work, especially in the early days. Instead of evaluating yourself solely on longer-term metrics, push yourself to make progress on something each day. Shoot for having a different problem each week. You can start by simply asking yourself and your team: did you have a good day? If you've had enough good days in a row, you're going in the right direction. Stay organized . Often, the amount of time required to stay a bit more organized can pay dividends down the road. Not only for yourself, but for your team. Personally, I love bringing structure to chaos, and I often reframe tasks as disorder to motivate myself. These tasks can be as diverse as writing product strategy documents, designing product specs in Figma, and refactoring parts of our codebase. At a startup, you can apply learnings immediately and truly adopt an experimentation oriented mindset to growth. I started off as a pre-med student in college, and then ended up doing my PhD in electrical engineering, and now I'm leading product for a creator economy company. There may not seem to be a pattern to my path, but it all is rooted in a love for learning. When that excitement comes from a deep internal source, I don't lose the passion even through tough times and evolving external conditions. ‍

Opportunity to evaluate a giant play where free gas appears to be trapped beneath the hydrate zone, defined by the Bottom Simulating Reflector (BSR).
